title: Deploy Your Own App
description: Build a personal trainer iOS app from scratch using Xcode and Claude Code

children.text: Led by **Jordan**

items: Install Xcode and Claude Desktop on your Mac
Create a new SwiftUI iOS project in Xcode
Connect your Xcode project to Claude Code
Build and test your personal trainer app in the iOS Simulator and on your iPhone
Use your AI tool as a UX thought partner to iterate on features
children.title: What you'll build

children.text: **What you need for this session**
Before we start, make sure you have these ready.

items: A Mac running macOS
Apple ID (free, needed for device signing)
~20GB of free disk space (Xcode is ~15GB)
iPhone (optional; the iOS Simulator works on its own)
Anthropic account at claude.ai

sections.title: 1. Installation & Setup
sections.subtitle: Install Xcode and Claude Desktop on your Mac

children.text: **What is Xcode?**

Xcode is Apple's official development environment for iOS, macOS, and other Apple platform apps. It includes a code editor, an iOS Simulator, a debugger, and the build system that compiles your Swift code and installs it on your device.

Claude Desktop is your AI coding partner. Once you point it at your Xcode project folder, it can read and write your Swift files directly, so you build features through conversation, not by typing code yourself.

items: **Xcode**: Apple's iOS development environment (~15GB from the App Store)
**Claude Desktop**: Your AI thought partner, connected to your project folder
children.title: What you're installing

children.text: Install Xcode

items: Open App Store on your Mac
Search for "Xcode"
Click **Get → Install**
Wait for installation to complete (this is large, ~15GB)
Open Xcode once installed
In the top nav, go to **Xcode → Settings → Locations**
Verify Command Line Tools are installed (should show a version number)

children.text: Install Claude Desktop

items: Download Claude Desktop from claude.ai
Click **Download for Mac**
Open the downloaded file and drag Claude to Applications folder
Launch Claude from Applications
Sign in with your Anthropic account

children.title: Can't install Xcode on macOS Sequoia (App Store blocks it)

children.text:
The App Store's current Xcode requires **macOS 26 (Tahoe)**, so on **macOS Sequoia 15** it simply won't install. The fix is to download **Xcode 26.3**, the most recent version that still supports **macOS 15.6+**, directly from Apple.

**1.** Make sure you're on **macOS 15.6 or later** (**Apple menu → System Settings → General → Software Update**). Xcode 26.3 won't run on older Sequoia.
**2.** Go to **developer.apple.com/download/all** and sign in with your free Apple ID.
**3.** Search for **Xcode 26.3** and download the **.xip** (large, ~10GB). Direct link: download.developer.apple.com/Developer_Tools/Xcode_26.3/Xcode_26.3_Universal.xip (you must be signed in for it to work).
**4.** Double-click the downloaded **.xip** to expand it (this takes a few minutes), then drag **Xcode** into your **Applications** folder.
**5.** Open Xcode once to finish first-launch setup, then continue with the rest of this session.

Heads up: even after this, the brand-new iOS Simulator won't run on Sequoia. See the **"Simulator won't launch on an older Mac"** note in Build 4 for the iOS 18 workaround.

**On macOS Sequoia 15?** The App Store only offers the newest Xcode, which **requires macOS 26 (Tahoe)**, so it won't install on Sequoia. You can still do this session: download a Sequoia-compatible Xcode (**26.3**, which supports **macOS 15.6+**) directly from Apple instead. Steps are in the **"Can't install Xcode on macOS Sequoia"** note at the bottom of this section.

sections.title: 2. Create a New iOS Project in Xcode
sections.subtitle: Configure and save your Xcode project for development

children.text: **SwiftUI: Apple's modern UI framework**

SwiftUI is Apple's declarative UI framework, introduced in 2019. You describe what the UI should look like and SwiftUI handles the rendering. UIKit is the older imperative approach.

For new projects, SwiftUI is the right choice: it's more concise, works better with AI-generated code, and is Apple's preferred path going forward. All the settings you'll select below are the defaults for a modern iOS app.

items: **Language:** Swift
**User Interface:** SwiftUI
**Lifecycle:** SwiftUI App
children.title: Key settings to select

children.text: Create a new project

items: Open Xcode
Click **File → New → Project**
Select **iOS** at the top
Choose **App** template
Click **Next**

children.text: Configure project settings

items: **Product Name:** Enter your app name (e.g., "PersonalTrainerApp")
**Team:** Select your team (or "None" if no team)
**Organization Identifier:** Enter your domain reversed (e.g., "com.yourname.personaltrainer")
**Bundle Identifier:** Should auto-populate
**Language:** Select Swift
**User Interface:** Select SwiftUI
**Lifecycle:** Select SwiftUI App
Click **Next**

children.text: Choose a save location

items: Select a folder on your Mac where you want the project stored
Make note of this path; you'll use it in Claude Code
Make sure **Add to:** shows your project
Click **Create**

children.text: Verify the project structure. In Xcode's left sidebar, you should see: **YourAppName/**, YourAppNameApp.swift, ContentView.swift, Assets.xcassets/, Preview Content/, and Info.plist

sections.title: 3. Connect Xcode Project to Claude Code
sections.subtitle: Open your project folder in Claude Desktop and select the right model

children.text: **How Claude Code reads your project**

Claude Code works by reading the files in your project folder directly. When you open a folder in Claude Desktop, your AI tool can see all your Swift files and project configuration, and it can write changes back to those files.

This is what makes the feedback loop work: your AI tool edits a file, Xcode picks up the change automatically, and you press **Command + R** to rebuild and test.

items: You open your Xcode project folder in Claude Desktop
Your AI tool reads your project's file structure
You send a prompt and your AI tool writes or edits Swift files
Xcode detects the file change automatically
You press **Command + R** to rebuild and test
children.title: The development loop

children.text: Get your project folder path

items: In Xcode, right-click on your project name in the left sidebar
Select **Show in Finder**
Copy the full folder path (**Command + Option + C** to copy path)
Keep Finder open; you'll need this path

children.text: Open the project in Claude Desktop

items: Open Claude Desktop app
Look for a folder icon or "Attach files" option
Select **Open Folder** or "Add Folder to Claude"
Navigate to your Xcode project folder and select it

children.text: Select the right model

items: In Claude Desktop, look for Model Selection (usually top-right or in settings)
Change from default to **Claude Opus 4.6**
Confirm the selection

children.text: Verify the connection

items: In a new message, type: "What files do you see in my project?"
Your AI tool should list your project files
If it does, you're connected and ready!

sections.title: 4. Build & Test Your Personal Trainer App
sections.subtitle: Send your first build prompt, then test in Simulator and on your iPhone

children.text: **Your AI tool as a thought partner**

Your AI tool is not just a code generator; it's your thought partner. Use it like you would a principal designer on your team.

The best results come from conversation, not just requests. After each build, test the feature on your device, note what feels good and what needs work, and message your AI tool: "I just tested [feature]. Here's what I think: [your feedback]. As a principal UX designer, what would you improve?"

Treat your AI tool as your collaborative architect throughout the process.

items: "Does this follow iOS design patterns?"
"How would you simplify this flow?"
"What's missing from a user experience perspective?"
"If you were a user, what frustrates you about this?"
"What should we polish next?"
children.title: Key questions to ask your AI tool

children.text: Copy the build prompt below and paste it into Claude Desktop to kick off your personal trainer app.

children.label: Build prompt
children.prompt:
You are a principal iOS app architect helping me build a personal trainer iOS app using SwiftUI and Xcode. We've just created a new iOS project. I want to build a comprehensive fitness application with these core features:

User Features:
- Users can set fitness goals (weight loss, muscle gain, endurance, flexibility, sleep, general fitness)
- Real-time health data integration from Apple Health (steps, sleep duration, calories burned, heart rate, weight, body fat)
- Function Health biomarker tracking integration
- AI-generated personalized training plans (weekly workouts tailored to goals)
- Personalized nutrition plans with macro/calorie targets
- Adaptive workout intensity based on daily check-ins (mood, energy, soreness, heart rate)
- Daily morning check-in prompts (mood, energy, soreness, sleep quality)
- Food logging with meal plans
- Streak system for consistency tracking with streak freezes
- Milestone celebrations at 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% goal completion
- Rewards & gamification system (points for workouts, check-ins, goal progress)
- Sign in with Apple authentication

Technical Requirements:
- SwiftUI with Swift 6 concurrency
- HealthKit integration for Apple Health data
- Supabase backend for user data (PostgreSQL)
- Local storage with UserDefaults for offline support
- No authentication barriers — focus on app experience first

Your Role: As a principal UX designer and architect, I want you to:
- Help me build this incrementally, starting with the core onboarding and dashboard
- After each feature build, ask me: "What should we focus on next?" or "What would improve the UX here?"
- Suggest design improvements as if you were reviewing the app
- Build features that look polished and production-ready
- Focus on user experience and engagement

Our Process:
- You'll guide me through building features in Xcode
- I'll test changes on my iOS device (we'll set that up)
- After each build, we'll review what looks good and what needs improvement
- We're NOT shipping to the App Store yet — just building for personal device testing

Let's start by building an engaging onboarding flow and dashboard. Show me the app structure, then ask: what should we build first after these core screens?
children.prompt_note: This sets your AI tool up as a principal iOS architect and UX designer. It establishes the full app vision, your iterative process, and how you want your AI tool to guide you through each build. Starting with onboarding and dashboard gives you a foundation to build on session after session.

children.text: Test your app in the iOS Simulator

items: In Xcode, click the device selector at the top (shows "iPhone 15" or similar)
Select **Simulator → iPhone 15 Pro** (or your preferred device)
Click the **Run** button (▶) to build and launch
Interact with your app: tap, scroll, and pinch-zoom with your trackpad

children.text: Test on your physical iPhone (optional)

items: Plug your iPhone into your Mac with a USB cable
Tap **Trust** on your iPhone when prompted
In Xcode, click your project name in the left sidebar
Go to **Targets → YourAppName → Signing & Capabilities**
Under **Team**, click **Add Account** if needed, then select your Apple ID (Xcode creates a free development certificate)
Select your iPhone from the device selector at the top of Xcode
Click **Run** (▶) and your app will install and open on your device

children.text: Iterate with your AI tool after each build

items: Test a feature on your device and note what feels good and what needs work
Message your AI tool: "I just tested [feature]. Here's what I think: [your feedback]. What would you improve?"
Your AI tool will suggest refinements and update the code
Press **Command + R** in Xcode to rebuild and test
Repeat until the feature is polished

children.text: Make a change in Claude Code → your AI tool saves files to your Xcode project → files auto-update in Xcode → press **Command + R** to rebuild → test on Simulator or device → report back with feedback → repeat.
children.title: Development loop

children.text:
**Xcode**
**Command + R**: Build and run
**Command + Shift + K**: Clean build
**Command + B**: Just build (don't run)
**Command + Option + Click**: Show code documentation
**Command + //**: Comment/uncomment code

**Simulator**
**Command + Shift + H**: Go to home screen
**Command + Shift + D**: Rotate device
**Command + Shift + R**: Reset simulator
**Command + Q**: Close simulator

**Claude Code tips**
Ask your AI tool to show you the code before applying changes. Request specific file locations: "Update ContentView.swift to...". Ask for explanations: "Explain how this HealthKit integration works".
children.title: Xcode & Simulator shortcuts reference

children.text: Press **Command + Shift + K** to clean, then **Command + B** to rebuild. Check for red error messages in the Issue Navigator (left sidebar). Share the error message with your AI tool for help.
Press **Command + Shift + K** to clean, then **Command + R** to rebuild fresh. If still stuck, close the Simulator and reopen it.
Unplug your device, plug it back in, and tap **Trust** on the device if prompted. In Xcode, reselect the device from the device selector and try building again.
In Xcode, go **Window → Devices and Simulators**. Select the Simulator and click **Erase All Content and Settings**. Then rebuild your project.

children.title: Simulator won't launch on an older Mac (no devices / runtime won't install)

children.text:
If your Mac is on an older macOS (e.g. **macOS Sequoia 15**) but you have the newest Xcode, the brand-new iOS Simulator can refuse to install: the device menu shows **"No devices"** or only "Any iOS Simulator Device," and you can't press Run. That's because the newest iOS Simulator needs the newest macOS to work; it has nothing to do with your app.

The fix is to run on an **iOS 18 Simulator** instead. Everything in this app works on iOS 18:

**1.** Lower your app's minimum iOS version. In Xcode, click your project in the left sidebar → select your app **target → General** tab → set **Minimum Deployments → iOS** to **18.0**. (Or just ask your AI tool: "Set the iOS deployment target to 18.0.")
**2.** Download an iOS 18 Simulator. Go **Xcode → Settings → Components**, find **iOS 18.x Simulator**, and click **Get** (it's a large download, ~7GB).
**3.** In the device selector at the top of Xcode, pick an **iPhone (iOS 18.5)** simulator and press **Command + R**.

Once you upgrade to the newest macOS later, you can raise the deployment target back up.

children.title: App installed on your iPhone but won't open ("Could not verify")

children.text:
With a **free** Apple ID, your iPhone has to verify the app with Apple the first time it runs, so it installs but won't open yet.

**1.** Turn on Developer Mode: **Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode**, toggle on, and restart when prompted.
**2.** Trust your certificate: **Settings → General → VPN & Device Management → [your Apple ID] → Trust**, then tap **Verify App**.

If **Verify App** keeps bouncing back to "Not Verified," your Wi-Fi is probably blocking Apple's check. Turn **Wi-Fi off** so you're on **cellular** and tap **Verify App** again, and it almost always clears on a clean connection. If it still won't cooperate, just use the **iOS Simulator** instead; it needs no signing or verification at all.

Note: free-account apps expire after 7 days; rerun from Xcode to refresh the signature.

**On an older Mac?** If you're on **macOS Sequoia (15) or earlier**, the brand-new iOS Simulator won't install: the device menu shows **"No devices"** and you can't press Run. It's not your app: the newest Simulator needs the newest macOS. The fix is to run on an **iOS 18 Simulator** instead (lower your deployment target to **iOS 18.0** and download the iOS 18 runtime). Full steps are in the **"Simulator won't launch on an older Mac"** troubleshooting note at the bottom of this section.

Connected your project folder to Claude Code
Sent your first build prompt and launched a personal trainer app
Tested your app in the iOS Simulator and (optionally) on your iPhone
Established an iterative build loop with your AI tool
children.title: What you built today

children.text:
**Next steps after initial setup**

1. **Test the initial build** on your device
2. **Take a screenshot** of what you see
3. **Report to your AI tool:** "I see [what's on screen]. I like [aspect]. I'd change [aspect]. What do you recommend?"
4. **Iterate** on design and features based on its suggestions
5. **Build incrementally**, one feature at a time
6. **Use your AI tool as your design partner**: ask for feedback, improvements, and what to build next

children.title: No Mac? Build it on the web instead

children.text:
You don't need a Mac, Xcode, or an iPhone for this workshop. You can build the same kind of app as a website that runs in any browser.

1. **Install Node.js** (nodejs.org) and a code editor like **VS Code** or **Cursor**, which run on Windows, Mac, or Linux. Or skip installs entirely with a browser tool like **bolt.new**, **v0**, or **Replit**.
2. **Create a project:** ask your AI tool to scaffold a **Vite + React** or **Next.js** app, or start from a template.
3. **Connect your AI tool** to the project folder just like above, then send the build prompt.
4. **Run it locally:** run **npm run dev** and open the **localhost** link in your browser. Changes hot-reload as you build.
5. **Deploy:** connect the project to **Vercel** or **Netlify** to get a public URL you can share.

One difference: a web app can't read Apple Health, so use **manual entry or sample data** for the health metrics. Everything else (goals, plans, nutrition, streaks) works the same.
